{{Short description|Periodic solution to the n-body problem}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''n''-body choreography}}	
An '''''n''-body choreography''' is a [[periodic function|periodic solution]] to the [[n-body problem]] in which all the bodies are equally spread out along a single [[orbit]].<ref name=Vanderbei>{{Cite journal | last1 = Vanderbei | first1 = Robert J. | doi = 10.1196/annals.1311.024 | title = New Orbits for the n-Body Problem | journal = Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences | volume = 1017 | issue = 1 | pages = 422–433 | year = 2004 | pmid =  15220160|arxiv = astro-ph/0303153 |bibcode = 2004NYASA1017..422V | citeseerx = 10.1.1.140.6108 | s2cid = 8202325 }}</ref> The term was originated in 2000 by Chenciner and Montgomery.<ref name=Vanderbei/><ref>Simó, C. [2000], [http://www.mathematik.uni-bielefeld.de/~rehmann/ECM/cdrom/3ecm/pdfs/pant3/simo.pdf New families of Solutions in N-Body Problems], Proceedings of the ECM 2000, Barcelona (July, 10-14).</ref><ref>[https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0011268 "A remarkable periodic solution of the three-body problem in the case of equal masses"]. The  original article by Alain Chenciner and Richard Montgomery.  Annals of Mathematics, 152 (2000), 881–901.</ref>  One such orbit is a [[circular orbit]], with equal masses at the corners of an [[equilateral triangle]]; another is the figure-8 orbit, first discovered numerically in 1993 by [[Cristopher Moore]]<ref name=Moore>{{cite journal | last=Moore | first=Cristopher | title=Braids in classical dynamics | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=70 | issue=24 | date=1993-06-14 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.70.3675 | pmid=10053934 | bibcode=1993PhRvL..70.3675M | pages=3675–3679}} Moore's numerical discovery of the figure-8 choreography using variational methods.</ref> and subsequently proved to exist by Chenciner and Montgomery.  Choreographies can be discovered using [[calculus of variations|variational methods]],<ref name=Vanderbei/> and more recently, [[Topology|topological]] approaches have been used to attempt a classification in the planar case.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Montaldi | first1=James | last2=Steckles | first2=Katerina | title=Classification of symmetry groups for planar n-body choreographies | journal=Forum of Mathematics, Sigma | publisher=Cambridge University Press (CUP) | volume=1 | year=2013 | issn=2050-5094 | doi=10.1017/fms.2013.5 | article-number=e5|arxiv=1305.0470| bibcode=2013arXiv1305.0470M |doi-access=free}}{{Creative Commons text attribution notice|cc=by3|from this source=yes}}
</ref> Having knowledge of specific solutions such as choreographies can be incredibly useful as it is not possible to solve the N-body problem for N > 2 through explicit means.

== Numerical Method ==
Numerical methods using computers have been crucial in the discovery and understanding of choreographies from their inception. In 1993, Moore employed a numerical implementation of the direct method from the calculus of variations to uncover the "eight" choreography. Later, during the rediscovery period between 1999 and 2000, Carles Simó dispelled doubts surrounding the validity of complex existence proofs through meticulous numerical investigations.<ref>{{Citation |last=Simó |first=Carles |title=Celestial Mechanics |chapter=Dynamical properties of the figure eight solution of the three-body problem |date=2002 |chapter-url=http://www.ams.org/conm/292/ |series=Contemporary Mathematics |volume=292 |pages=209–228 |editor-last=Chenciner |editor-first=Alain |access-date=2023-05-05 |place=Providence, Rhode Island |publisher=American Mathematical Society |language=en |doi=10.1090/conm/292/04926 |isbn=978-0-8218-2902-8 |editor2-last=Cushman |editor2-first=Richard |editor3-last=Robinson |editor3-first=Clark |editor4-last=Xia |editor4-first=Zhihong Jeff}}</ref>

The numerical implementation process can be distilled into a gradient search within a finite-dimensional approximation of the path space. One approach involves discretizing the path at uniform time intervals. Another effective method entails expressing the action as a function of the Fourier components of the choreography curve and truncating the [[Fourier series]] at a finite order. Convergence can be verified by increasing the truncation order and observing the alterations in the resulting minimizing Fourier coefficients. If these changes fall within a specified tolerance range, the result can be considered successful. For further refinements, consult the works of Simó or Moore and Nauenberg. <ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Moore |first1=Cristopher |last2=Nauenberg |first2=Michael |date=2008-10-17 |title=New Periodic Orbits for the n-Body Problem |eprint=math/0511219 }}</ref>

=== Topological Method ===
In 2013, Montaldi and Steckles categorized all possible symmetry groups of planar 𝑛-body collision-free choreographies, which can be divided into two infinite families and, in the case of odd values of 𝑛, three exceptional groups. The second part of their study involves the development of the equivariant [[fundamental group]], which is employed to identify the topology of the space of loops possessing a particular symmetry. They demonstrate that this topology is linked to certain [[Coset|cosets]] of the pure [[braid group]] in the full braid group, as well as the centralizers of elements within the corresponding coset. Furthermore, their work refines the symmetry classification by categorizing the connected components of the set of loops with a given symmetry, leading to the discovery of many new choreographies in 𝑛-body systems that are governed by a strong force potential.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Montaldi |first1=James |last2=Steckles |first2=Katrina |title=Classification of Symmetry Groups for Planar -Body Choreographies |date=2013 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/forum-of-mathematics-sigma/article/classification-of-symmetry-groups-for-planar-nbody-choreographies/710D0EC787DED736B64A94D0E5CD01E1 |journal=Forum of Mathematics, Sigma |language=en |volume=1 |article-number=e5 |doi=10.1017/fms.2013.5 |s2cid=119143933 |issn=2050-5094|arxiv=1305.0470 }}</ref>
